lines.text: You can separate your waste [afval scheiden].
That is better for the milieu: you help keep the air and water clean, and a lot of waste (such as glass) can be used again.
Anyone who throws waste on the street can get a fine [boete] — also if you, for example, put cardboard [karton] next to the container.
Own containers: in most municipalities, people in a single-family house [eengezinswoning] have different containers:
for gft: vegetable, fruit and garden waste,
for paper,
for plastic and packaging [verpakkingen],
for all other waste: the residual waste [restafval].
The containers have colors, for example green for gft, blue for paper, gray for residual waste and orange for plastic — different per municipality.
The waste is collected on fixed days [vaste dagen].
Only on those days (usually also the evening before) may you put the container out on the street, otherwise you can get a fine.
No own containers: in a flat, you put the residual waste in bags in a container on the street.
Often you can also separate waste there (paper, glass, sometimes plastic and gft), whenever you want.
Old clothing goes into clothing containers [kledingcontainers].
Chemical waste [Chemisch afval], such as batteries, must be brought to special places run by the municipality.
Glass and plastic bottles and cans [blikjes] often have a deposit [statiegeld]: you pay when buying and get the money back when you return [inlevert] the bottle, for example at the supermarket.
If a glass bottle has no deposit, it goes into the glass container [glasbak].
Bulky waste [Groot afval], such as a sofa, can be picked up; you must pay for that and make an appointment.
Tax: for the collection of waste you pay tax to the municipality: the waste collection charge [afvalstoffenheffing].
For the waste water [afvalwater] — water that goes through your sewer [riool] — you pay a sewage charge [rioolheffing].
With a low income you can usually get a discount [korting] or remission [kwijtschelding]; with remission you pay nothing.
